arXiv:2609.15651v1 [math.CO] 14 Sep 2026

Multivariate stability of powered triangular recurrences
and parametrised Eulerian polynomials

Umesh Shankar Affiliation: Department of Computer Science and Automation, Affiliation: Indian Institute of Science Bengaluru, Affiliation: Bengaluru 560012, Karnataka, India Affiliation: Email: umeshshankar@outlook.com
September 14, 2026
Abstract

We prove multivariate stability for a class of affine triangular recurrences whose two coefficients are raised to an arbitrary positive integer power. The variables keep track of cross-step heights in a weighted lattice-path model. The applications include stability and real-rootedness of parametrised Eulerian, Stirling, and Lah families. For the parametrised Eulerian polynomials, we obtain multivariate refinements of known real-rootedness results and prove simplicity and strict interlacing of consecutive rows. A kernel-preserving bijection with increasing binary trees yields a synchronised Foata–Strehl action on pairs and a combinatorial interpretation of their gamma coefficients along with a recurrence. The same bijection identifies refinement posets that admit symmetric Boolean and chain decompositions for parameter one and cover-supported 𝔰​𝔩2\mathfrak{sl}_{2} operators prove their PECKness. We extend the stability and strict interlacing results to synchronised Stirling permutations and prove PECKness for ordinary Stirling permutations with a fixed number of plateaux.

Keywords: stable polynomial; triangular recurrence; Eulerian polynomial; Stirling permutation; gamma-positivity; symmetric chain decomposition.

Introduction

For a positive integer nn, let [n]={1,2,…,n}[n]=\{1,2,\dots,n\} and let 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n} denote the set of permutations of [n][n]. For π=π1π2⋯πn∈𝔖n\pi=\pi_{1}\pi_{2}\cdots\pi_{n}\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}, let DES⁡(π)={i∈[n−1]:πi>πi+1}\DES(\pi)=\{i\in[n-1]:\pi_{i}>\pi_{i+1}\} be its descent set and let des⁡(π)=|DES⁡(π)|\des(\pi)=|\DES(\pi)|. Similarly, let EXC⁡(π)={i∈[n]:πi>i}\EXC(\pi)=\{i\in[n]:\pi_{i}>i\} and exc⁡(π)=|EXC⁡(π)|\exc(\pi)=|\EXC(\pi)| be its excedance set and number of excedances. The nnth Eulerian polynomial is

An​(t)=∑π∈𝔖ntdes⁡(π).A_{n}(t)=\sum_{\pi\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}t^{\des(\pi)}.

It also enumerates permutations by excedances: An​(t)=∑π∈𝔖ntexc⁡(π)A_{n}(t)=\sum_{\pi\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}t^{\exc(\pi)}. These polynomials and their many interpretations are treated in Petersen’s book [19].

A polynomial p⁡(t)=∑k=0dak​tkp(t)=\sum_{k=0}^{d}a_{k}t^{k} is palindromic if ak=ad−ka_{k}=a_{d-k} for every 1≤k≤d1\leq k\leq d. Every such polynomial has a unique expansion

p⁡(t)=∑j=0⌊d/2⌋γj​tj​(1+t)d−2​j.p(t)=\sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor d/2\rfloor}\gamma_{j}t^{j}(1+t)^{d-2j}.

It is gamma-positive if all γj\gamma_{j} are nonnegative. A real polynomial is real-rooted if all its zeros are real. The ordinary Eulerian polynomials are palindromic, gamma-positive, and real-rooted [19]. Multivariate refinements retain additional information about the descent statistic. A polynomial with real coefficients is real stable if it is nonzero whenever all its variables lie in the open upper half-plane. The following result is one such refinement due to Haglund and Visontai [14].

Theorem ([14, Theorem 3.2]).

Put π0=πn+1=0\pi_{0}=\pi_{n+1}=0 for π∈𝔖n\pi\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}. The polynomial

ℰn​(𝐱,𝐲)=∑π∈𝔖n∏1≤i≤nπi>πi+1xπi​∏1≤i≤nπi−1<πiyπi\mathcal{E}_{n}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})=\sum_{\pi\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq i\leq n\\ \pi_{i}>\pi_{i+1}\end{subarray}}x_{\pi_{i}}\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq i\leq n\\ \pi_{i-1}<\pi_{i}\end{subarray}}y_{\pi_{i}}

is real stable.

The terminal descent is included in this convention, so setting xi=tx_{i}=t and yi=1y_{i}=1 gives t​An​(t)tA_{n}(t).

The Eulerian numbers A⁡(n,k)A(n,k), which are the coefficients of An​(t)A_{n}(t), satisfy

A⁡(n,k)=(k+1)​A​(n−1,k)+(n−k)​A​(n−1,k−1)(n≥2),A(n,k)=(k+1)A(n-1,k)+(n-k)A(n-1,k-1)\qquad(n\geq 2),

with A⁡(1,0)=1A(1,0)=1 and zero entries outside 0≤k≤n−10\leq k\leq n-1. In [22], an ℓ\ell-parametrised generalisation was defined by raising the two recurrence coefficients to the positive integer power ℓ\ell. These numbers count ℓ\ell-tuples of subexceedant functions with a common block-leader set. Shankar proved palindromicity and log-concavity, established gamma-positivity for ℓ=2\ell=2, and proposed real-rootedness and gamma-positivity for the remaining powers.

We write An,ℓ​(t)=∑kAℓ​(n,k)​tkA_{n,\ell}(t)=\sum_{k}A_{\ell}(n,k)t^{k}, where

Aℓ​(n,k)=(k+1)ℓ​Aℓ​(n−1,k)+(n−k)ℓ​Aℓ​(n−1,k−1),Aℓ​(1,0)=1,A_{\ell}(n,k)=(k+1)^{\ell}A_{\ell}(n-1,k)+(n-k)^{\ell}A_{\ell}(n-1,k-1),\qquad A_{\ell}(1,0)=1,

and entries outside 0≤k≤n−10\leq k\leq n-1 are zero. Palindromicity gives the unique expansion

An,ℓ​(t)=∑j=0⌊(n−1)/2⌋γn,ℓ,j​tj​(1+t)n−1−2​j.A_{n,\ell}(t)=\sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor(n-1)/2\rfloor}\gamma_{n,\ell,j}t^{j}(1+t)^{n-1-2j}. (I.1)

Write Γn,ℓ​(u)=∑jγn,ℓ,j​uj\Gamma_{n,\ell}(u)=\sum_{j}\gamma_{n,\ell,j}u^{j} for its gamma-polynomial. The following univariate results are due to Alexandersson [1].

Theorem (Alexandersson [1, Theorem 5.1]).

For positive integers nn and ℓ\ell, both An,ℓA_{n,\ell} and Γn,ℓ\Gamma_{n,\ell} are real-rooted, and Γn,ℓ\Gamma_{n,\ell} has nonnegative coefficients. The rows An,ℓA_{n,\ell} and An+1,ℓA_{n+1,\ell} weakly interlace.

Alexandersson’s proof divides the degree-kk coefficient by (n−1k)ℓ\binom{n-1}{k}^{\ell} and restores the original coefficients by a Hadamard-product argument. A similar normalisation argument also appears in [23]. Our main stability theorem extends this normalisation to powered affine recurrences and a polynomial that keeps track of a separate variable for each cross-step height. For the Eulerian specialisation, we also prove simplicity and strict interlacing. The tree actions and refinement posets provide combinatorial structures for these polynomial families.

Stability criteria for recursive polynomials and their interlacing consequences were developed by Ding and Zhu [9]. Yang and Zhang [27] constructed stable refinements of Narayana and second-order Eulerian polynomials using labelled plane trees. Our variables record cross-step heights in the insertion history. The six sections below develop the relevant combinatorial models, the general stability theorem, and its Eulerian and Stirling applications. We state the main results here.

A subexceedant function f:[n]→[n]f:[n]\to[n] is a function that satisfies f⁡(i)≤if(i)\leq i. Its kernel is the partition into classes sharing the same image, and bl⁡(f)\bl(f) is the set of their minima. Let 𝒬n,ℓ\mathcal{Q}_{n,\ell} consist of ℓ\ell-tuples with a common set BB of block minima, ordered by proper kernel refinement in every coordinate, with equality added. Let 𝒯n,ℓ\mathcal{T}_{n,\ell} consist of ℓ\ell-tuples of increasing plane binary trees on [n][n] with a common set LL of left-child labels.

In Section 1, we construct the bijection that takes the tuples of subexceedant functions counted by parametrised Eulerian numbers to tuples of synchronised increasing plane binary trees. Additionally, we also give a natural poset on these objects.

Theorem A (Combinatorial models).
  1. (i)

    There is a bijection Φn:𝒬n,1→𝒯n,1\Phi_{n}:\mathcal{Q}_{n,1}\to\mathcal{T}_{n,1} under which the blocks of ker⁡(f)\ker(f) are the vertex sets of the maximal right chains of Φn​(f)\Phi_{n}(f). In particular, L⁡(Φn​(f))=bl⁡(f)∖{1}L(\Phi_{n}(f))=\bl(f)\setminus\{1\}. Its coordinatewise extension is a bijection 𝒬n,ℓ→𝒯n,ℓ\mathcal{Q}_{n,\ell}\to\mathcal{T}_{n,\ell}, and

    An,ℓ​(t)=∑𝐓∈𝒯n,ℓt|L⁡(𝐓)|.A_{n,\ell}(t)=\sum_{\mathbf{T}\in\mathcal{T}_{n,\ell}}t^{|L(\mathbf{T})|}. (I.2)
  2. (ii)

    The poset 𝒬n,ℓ\mathcal{Q}_{n,\ell} is bounded and graded of rank n−1n-1, with rank function ρ⁡(𝐟)=|B⁡(𝐟)|−1\rho(\mathbf{f})=|B(\mathbf{f})|-1 and rank-generating polynomial An,ℓ​(t)A_{n,\ell}(t).

Assume

and an​(j),bn​(j)>0a_{n}(j),b_{n}(j)>0 for n>n0n>n_{0} and 0≤j≤n−n0−10\leq j\leq n-n_{0}-1. Suppose also that

The proof in Section 2 balances the two path extensions and applies finite Pólya–Schur theory and hypergeometric zero locations. Table 1 lists the covered sequence families. We also remark on some extensions to general triangular arrays.

For the Eulerian recurrence, write Fn,ℓF_{n,\ell} for the cross-step refinement defined above with initial vertex (0,1)(0,1). Thus, a variable ziz_{i} marks a common block minimum i>1i>1. Write Pn,ℓP_{n,\ell} for the polynomial obtained by dividing its degree-kk coefficients by (n−1k)ℓ\binom{n-1}{k}^{\ell}, and put A^n,ℓ​(t)=Pn,ℓ​(t,…,t)\widehat{A}_{n,\ell}(t)=P_{n,\ell}(t,\ldots,t).

Theorem C (Eulerian stability and strict interlacing).

For all positive integers n,ℓn,\ell, the following assertions hold.

  1. (i)

    Both Fn,ℓF_{n,\ell} and Pn,ℓP_{n,\ell} are real stable. The polynomials An,ℓA_{n,\ell}, A^n,ℓ\widehat{A}_{n,\ell}, and Fn,ℓ​(λ2​t,…,λn​t)F_{n,\ell}(\lambda_{2}t,\ldots,\lambda_{n}t) for λi>0\lambda_{i}>0 have only negative real zeros. The common block-minimum set of a uniformly chosen synchronised tuple, with 11 removed, has a strongly Rayleigh distribution.

  2. (ii)

    For fixed ℓ\ell, An,ℓA_{n,\ell} has simple zeros for n≥2n\geq 2. For n≥2n\geq 2, if α1<⋯<αn−1\alpha_{1}<\cdots<\alpha_{n-1} and β1<⋯<βn\beta_{1}<\cdots<\beta_{n} are the zeros of An,ℓA_{n,\ell} and An+1,ℓA_{n+1,\ell}, then

    β1<α1<β2<⋯<βn−1<αn−1<βn<0.\beta_{1}<\alpha_{1}<\beta_{2}<\cdots<\beta_{n-1}<\alpha_{n-1}<\beta_{n}<0. (I.3)

    The polynomial An+1,ℓ​(t)+z​An,ℓ​(t)A_{n+1,\ell}(t)+zA_{n,\ell}(t) is real stable. For every s∈ℝs\in\mathbb{R}, An+1,ℓ+s​An,ℓA_{n+1,\ell}+sA_{n,\ell} has simple real zeros. All are negative if s>−1s>-1; one is zero if s=−1s=-1; and exactly one is positive if s<−1s<-1.

Here a probability measure on subsets is strongly Rayleigh if its multiaffine generating polynomial is real stable [3]. Stability in Theorem C(i) is a direct application of Theorem B. Section 3 proves strict interlacing using intermediate interlacers and records the standard gamma-positivity consequences of real-rootedness and palindromicity.

In the next section, we focus on the case ℓ=2\ell=2. For a synchronised pair of trees, join two nonroot labels when they are siblings in either tree. This sibling graph is a union of paths and even cycles. Call the pair reduced when each odd component CC has exactly (|C|−1)/2(|C|-1)/2 left-child labels. There is no restriction on the orientations of even components.

Theorem D (Gamma coefficients for pairs).
  1. (i)

    Flipping the left–right statuses of all labels in an odd sibling component, simultaneously in both trees, defines commuting involutions. Each orbit has a unique reduced pair. If this pair has kk common left-child labels, the orbit enumerator is

    ∑𝐒∈𝒪t|L⁡(𝐒)|=tk​(1+t)n−1−2​k.\sum_{\mathbf{S}\in\mathcal{O}}t^{|L(\mathbf{S})|}=t^{k}(1+t)^{n-1-2k}. (I.4)

    Consequently, γn,2,k\gamma_{n,2,k} counts reduced pairs with kk common left-child labels, and γn,2,0=1\gamma_{n,2,0}=1.

  2. (ii)

    With γ1,2,0=1\gamma_{1,2,0}=1 and coefficients outside their support equal to zero, for n≥2n\geq 2 one has

    γn,2,k=(k+1)2​γn−1,2,k+(n−2​k)​(n+2​k+1)​γn−1,2,k−1.\gamma_{n,2,k}=(k+1)^{2}\gamma_{n-1,2,k}+(n-2k)(n+2k+1)\gamma_{n-1,2,k-1}. (I.5)

Section 4 constructs the action and proves the recurrence. We mention how the action recovers the ordinary unary-tree action when ℓ=1\ell=1. The gamma-positivity for ℓ=2\ell=2 was proved in [22]. Our Theorem D here gives the orbit interpretation of its coefficients.

A finite graded poset is PECK if it is rank-symmetric, rank-unimodal, and strongly Sperner. The last condition says that the largest union of kk antichains has the size of the kk largest ranks, for every kk. A symmetric Boolean (respectively, chain) decomposition partitions the poset into Boolean subposets (respectively, saturated chains) whose endpoint ranks sum to its rank.

Theorem E (PECKness and symmetric decompositions).

For every n≥1n\geq 1, 𝒬n,1\mathcal{Q}_{n,1} admits a symmetric Boolean decomposition and a symmetric chain decomposition. On its tree basis, let EE sum the moves of a unary right child to the left, let FF sum the reverse moves, and set H​T=(2​ρ​(T)−n+1)​THT=(2\rho(T)-n+1)T. These operators define an 𝔰​𝔩2\mathfrak{sl}_{2}-representation, with EE supported on upward covers and FF on downward covers. In particular, 𝒬n,1\mathcal{Q}_{n,1} is PECK.

The operators and decompositions are proved in Section 5. Palindromicity and Theorem C(i) give rank symmetry and unimodality for all ℓ\ell. We propose the remaining order-theoretic conjecture.

Conjecture 1.

For every n≥1n\geq 1 and integer ℓ>1\ell>1, the poset 𝒬n,ℓ\mathcal{Q}_{n,\ell} is PECK.

Finally, an mm-Stirling permutation is a permutation of {1m,…,nm}\{1^{m},\ldots,n^{m}\} with no smaller letter between consecutive occurrences of a letter. Let d⁡(σ)d(\sigma) count the number of internal descents. Its descent history records whether this number increases when the block of copies of ii is inserted, for i=2,…,ni=2,\ldots,n. Let Fn,ℓ(m)F^{(m)}_{n,\ell} enumerate tuples with the same history, with ziz_{i} marking an increase at step ii, and let Sn,ℓ(m)​(t)=Fn,ℓ(m)​(t,…,t)S^{(m)}_{n,\ell}(t)=F^{(m)}_{n,\ell}(t,\ldots,t). Use maps f:[n]→[m⁡(n−1)+1]f:[n]\to[m(n-1)+1] satisfying f⁡(i)≤m⁡(i−1)+1f(i)\leq m(i-1)+1 to define the synchronised kernel-refinement poset ℛn,ℓ(m)\mathcal{R}^{(m)}_{n,\ell}.

Theorem F (Stirling extensions).

For positive integers m,ℓ,nm,\ell,n, the following assertions hold.

  1. (i)

    Fn,ℓ(m)F^{(m)}_{n,\ell} is real stable and its history distribution is strongly Rayleigh. For fixed m,ℓm,\ell, the polynomials Sn,ℓ(m)S^{(m)}_{n,\ell} have simple negative zeros and consecutive members strictly interlace. Their coefficients are log-concave and unimodal. The row pencil Sn+1,ℓ(m)​(t)+z​Sn,ℓ(m)​(t)S^{(m)}_{n+1,\ell}(t)+zS^{(m)}_{n,\ell}(t) is real stable; its real combinations have the same zero-sign alternatives as in Theorem C(iii).

  2. (ii)

    The bounded functions above are in bijection with increasing (m+1)(m+1)-ary trees, with kernel blocks corresponding to maximal chains in the rightmost slot. Under the Gessel correspondence, non-root block leaders are the insertion labels that increase the descent number. The poset ℛn,ℓ(m)\mathcal{R}^{(m)}_{n,\ell} is graded of rank n−1n-1, with rank polynomial Sn,ℓ(m)S^{(m)}_{n,\ell}.

The stability assertion is another application of Theorem B, recorded in Table 1. Section 6 proves the remaining assertions and discusses variable multiplicities. These polynomials record insertion histories, rather than the final descent-top sets used in [14].

For ordinary Stirling permutations (m=2m=2), let ℛn,p\mathcal{R}_{n,p} be the induced subposet of ℛn,1(2)\mathcal{R}^{(2)}_{n,1} with exactly pp plateaux, where a plateau is an adjacent equal pair. In the ternary-tree model, fix all parent relations, middle edges, and the order at doubly occupied outer slots; forget the orientations at singly occupied outer slots. Call this an outer-slot skeleton.

Theorem G (Fixed-plateau posets).

For 1≤p≤n1\leq p\leq n, the poset ℛn,p\mathcal{R}_{n,p} is graded of rank p−1p-1, with rank function ρp​(σ)=d⁡(σ)−(n−p)\rho_{p}(\sigma)=d(\sigma)-(n-p). It admits symmetric Boolean and chain decompositions and cover-supported 𝔰​𝔩2\mathfrak{sl}_{2} raising and lowering operators. In particular, it is PECK. Its rank polynomial is

t−(n−p)​∑plat⁡(σ)=ptd⁡(σ)=∑b=0⌊(p−1)/2⌋gn,p,b​tb​(1+t)p−1−2​b,t^{-(n-p)}\sum_{\operatorname{plat}(\sigma)=p}t^{d(\sigma)}=\sum_{b=0}^{\lfloor(p-1)/2\rfloor}g_{n,p,b}\,t^{b}(1+t)^{p-1-2b}, (I.6)

where gn,p,bg_{n,p,b} counts outer-slot skeletons with bb doubly occupied outer pairs.

The partial gamma expansion and its tree action are known [18, 7]. The final part of Section 6 proves their compatibility with kernel refinement, which gives the PECK and decomposition assertions.

1 Subexceedant functions, trees, and posets

We prove Theorem A by relating subexceedant functions, increasing binary trees, and kernel-refinement posets. We first recall the definition of the parametrised Eulerian polynomials. We write Aℓ​(n,k)A_{\ell}(n,k) for the family denoted by A1(ℓ)​(n,k)A^{(\ell)}_{1}(n,k) in [22]. These parametrised Eulerian numbers satisfy the recurrence [22, Proposition 18]

Aℓ​(n,k)=(k+1)ℓ​Aℓ​(n−1,k)+(n−k)ℓ​Aℓ​(n−1,k−1)(n≥2),A_{\ell}(n,k)=(k+1)^{\ell}A_{\ell}(n-1,k)+(n-k)^{\ell}A_{\ell}(n-1,k-1)\qquad(n\geq 2), (1.1)

with Aℓ​(1,0)=1A_{\ell}(1,0)=1 and Aℓ​(n,k)=0A_{\ell}(n,k)=0 for k∉{0,…,n−1}k\notin\{0,\ldots,n-1\}. We write

An,ℓ​(t)=∑k=0n−1Aℓ​(n,k)​tk.A_{n,\ell}(t)=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}A_{\ell}(n,k)t^{k}.

When ℓ=1\ell=1, these are the ordinary Eulerian polynomials, with the convention that the exponent records the number of descents. The first nonconstant rows are

A2,ℓ​(t)\displaystyle A_{2,\ell}(t) =1+t,\displaystyle=1+t,
A3,ℓ​(t)\displaystyle A_{3,\ell}(t) =1+2ℓ+1​t+t2,\displaystyle=1+2^{\ell+1}t+t^{2},
A4,ℓ​(t)\displaystyle A_{4,\ell}(t) =1+(2⋅4ℓ+3ℓ)​t+(2⋅4ℓ+3ℓ)​t2+t3.\displaystyle=1+(2\cdot 4^{\ell}+3^{\ell})t+(2\cdot 4^{\ell}+3^{\ell})t^{2}+t^{3}.

1.1 Subexceedant functions and parametrised Eulerian numbers

We use the subexceedant-function model introduced by Shankar [22, p. 5 and Section 4]. A subexceedant function on [n][n] is a map f:[n]→[n]f:[n]\to[n] satisfying f⁡(i)≤if(i)\leq i for every ii. We also write it as the word f(1)⋯f(n)f(1)\cdots f(n). Its kernel ker⁡(f)\ker(f) is the partition of [n][n] into nonempty sets of positions having the same image under ff. The block-leader set is

bl⁡(f)={i∈[n]:f⁡(i)∉f⁡([i−1])},\bl(f)=\{i\in[n]:f(i)\notin f([i-1])\},

where f⁡([0])=∅f([0])=\varnothing. Therefore, bl⁡(f)\bl(f) is the set of minima of the kernel blocks. Let

𝒬n,ℓ={(f1,…,fℓ):fa​ is subexceedant and ​bl⁡(f1)=⋯=bl⁡(fℓ)}.\mathcal{Q}_{n,\ell}=\{(f_{1},\ldots,f_{\ell}):f_{a}\text{ is subexceedant and }\bl(f_{1})=\cdots=\bl(f_{\ell})\}.

We call such tuples synchronised. For 𝐟∈𝒬n,ℓ\mathbf{f}\in\mathcal{Q}_{n,\ell}, write B⁡(𝐟)B(\mathbf{f}) for its common block-minimum set. We identify 𝒬n,1\mathcal{Q}_{n,1} with the set of subexceedant functions on [n][n].

Recall Shankar’s enumeration [22], whose proof also identifies the two extension weights used below.

Proposition 1.1.

The number of tuples 𝐟∈𝒬n,ℓ\mathbf{f}\in\mathcal{Q}_{n,\ell} with |B⁡(𝐟)|=k+1|B(\mathbf{f})|=k+1 is Aℓ​(n,k)A_{\ell}(n,k).

Proof.

We begin by restricting a tuple to [n−1][n-1]. If nn is not a new block minimum, each coordinate repeats one of its k+1k+1 existing values, giving (k+1)ℓ(k+1)^{\ell} extensions. If nn is a new block minimum, the restricted tuple has kk blocks. Each coordinate chooses one of the n−kn-k values in [n][n] not previously used, giving (n−k)ℓ(n-k)^{\ell} extensions. The resulting recurrence is (1.1), with the same initial condition. ∎

Encode a set B⊆[n]B\subseteq[n] containing 11 by the binary word e=(e2,…,en)e=(e_{2},\ldots,e_{n}), where ei=1e_{i}=1 if and only if i∈Bi\in B. Write |e|=∑i=2nei|e|=\sum_{i=2}^{n}e_{i}, and define

c(e)=∏i=2n(1+|{j:2≤j<i,ej≠ei}|),c(e)=\prod_{i=2}^{n}\left(1+\bigl|\{j:2\leq j<i,\ e_{j}\neq e_{i}\}\bigr|\right), (1.2)

with the empty product equal to 11.

The following is a combinatorial proof of palindromicity of the parametrised Eulerian polynomials.

Proposition 1.2.

For every binary word ee, the number of subexceedant functions whose block-minimum set is {1}∪{i:ei=1}\{1\}\cup\{i:e_{i}=1\} equals c⁡(e)c(e). Consequently,

An,ℓ​(t)=∑e∈{0,1}n−1c​(e)ℓ​t|e|.A_{n,\ell}(t)=\sum_{e\in\{0,1\}^{n-1}}c(e)^{\ell}t^{|e|}. (1.3)

The polynomial An,ℓA_{n,\ell} is monic and palindromic of degree n−1n-1, with constant coefficient 11 and positive coefficients in every degree.

Proof.

Suppose that the values through position i−1i-1 have been chosen, and put di=1+∑j=2i−1ejd_{i}=1+\sum_{j=2}^{i-1}e_{j}. If ei=0e_{i}=0, there are did_{i} previously used values available. If ei=1e_{i}=1, there are i−dii-d_{i} unused values in [i][i]. Both numbers equal the corresponding factor in (1.2). Multiplying these choices proves the count and independence of the ℓ\ell coordinates proves (1.3).

Complementing all bits leaves c⁡(e)c(e) unchanged and replaces |e||e| by n−1−|e|n-1-|e|, proving palindromicity. The constant words have weight 11, so the constant and leading coefficients are 11. Every word has positive weight, and words occur in every possible weight |e||e|. ∎

We retain the individual block-minimum labels in the multiaffine refinement

Fn,ℓ(z2,…,zn)=∑e∈{0,1}n−1c(e)ℓ∏i:ei=1zi.F_{n,\ell}(z_{2},\ldots,z_{n})=\sum_{e\in\{0,1\}^{n-1}}c(e)^{\ell}\prod_{i:e_{i}=1}z_{i}. (1.4)

Its diagonal specialisation is An,ℓ​(t)A_{n,\ell}(t).

1.2 A kernel-preserving tree interpretation

An increasing plane binary tree on [n][n] is a rooted tree whose vertices are labelled by [n][n], whose edges increase away from the root, and in which every vertex has at most one left child and at most one right child. Its root has label 11. Write 𝒯n\mathcal{T}_{n} for the set of these trees, and let L⁡(T)⊆{2,…,n}L(T)\subseteq\{2,\ldots,n\} be the set of labels of left children in TT. A maximal right chain is a connected component of the graph obtained by deleting all left edges. Its labels occur in increasing order from its root.

An ordered tuple 𝐓=(T1,…,Tℓ)∈𝒯nℓ\mathbf{T}=(T_{1},\ldots,T_{\ell})\in\mathcal{T}_{n}^{\ell} is said to be synchronised if

L⁡(T1)=⋯=L⁡(Tℓ).L(T_{1})=\cdots=L(T_{\ell}).

Let 𝒯n,ℓ\mathcal{T}_{n,\ell} be the set of such tuples and write L⁡(𝐓)L(\mathbf{T}) for their common left-child set.

The bijection in Theorem A(i) preserves the entire kernel partition. This additional property will allow us to interpret tree moves as relations in the posets considered below.

Proof of Theorem A(i).

We start by fixing a partition π={B1,…,Bs}\pi=\{B_{1},\ldots,B_{s}\} of [n][n], with its blocks ordered so that

1=b1<b2<⋯<bs,bj=min⁡Bj.1=b_{1}<b_{2}<\cdots<b_{s},\qquad b_{j}=\min B_{j}.

A subexceedant function with kernel π\pi is specified by distinct values a1,…,asa_{1},\ldots,a_{s}, where aj∈[bj]a_{j}\in[b_{j}], by setting f⁡(i)=ajf(i)=a_{j} for i∈Bji\in B_{j}. a1=1a_{1}=1 is forced. After a1,…,aj−1a_{1},\ldots,a_{j-1} have been chosen, the available values for aja_{j} form the ordered set

Ij=[bj]∖{a1,…,aj−1},|Ij|=bj−j+1.I_{j}=[b_{j}]\setminus\{a_{1},\ldots,a_{j-1}\},\qquad|I_{j}|=b_{j}-j+1.

We form a right chain from each block BjB_{j}, listing its vertices in increasing order. For j=2,…,sj=2,\ldots,s, we attach the root bjb_{j} of the jjth chain as a left child of a vertex pj<bjp_{j}<b_{j} whose left-child position is still unused. The available parent labels form the ordered set

Jj=[bj−1]∖{p2,…,pj−1},|Jj|=bj−j+1.J_{j}=[b_{j}-1]\setminus\{p_{2},\ldots,p_{j-1}\},\qquad|J_{j}|=b_{j}-j+1.

We choose pjp_{j} to have the same position in JjJ_{j} as aja_{j} has in IjI_{j}, where both sets are ordered increasingly. All newly added edges can only increase labels, every vertex other than 11 has exactly one parent, and no left-child position is used twice. Thus the result is an increasing plane binary tree. Its right chains are precisely the chains prescribed by π\pi.

In the other direction, the maximal right chains of a tree recover π\pi and their nonroot chain roots recover the parent labels p2,…,psp_{2},\ldots,p_{s}. Starting with a1=1a_{1}=1, we recover aja_{j} from the position of pjp_{j} in JjJ_{j} by choosing the value in the same position in IjI_{j}. This inverts the construction. The roots of the nonroot right chains are exactly the left children, proving the assertion about L​(Φn​(f))L(\Phi_{n}(f)). The coordinatewise extension and (I.2) follow from this. ∎

Example 1.3.

Consider f=113223∈𝒬6,1f=113223\in\mathcal{Q}_{6,1}. Its kernel blocks, in order of their minima, are

B1={1,2},B2={3,6},B3={4,5},B_{1}=\{1,2\},\qquad B_{2}=\{3,6\},\qquad B_{3}=\{4,5\},

and their values are (a1,a2,a3)=(1,3,2)(a_{1},a_{2},a_{3})=(1,3,2). For the root b2=3b_{2}=3, the available values and parents are I2={2,3}I_{2}=\{2,3\} and J2={1,2}J_{2}=\{1,2\}; thus a2=3a_{2}=3 selects p2=2p_{2}=2. For b3=4b_{3}=4, they are I3={2,4}I_{3}=\{2,4\} and J3={1,3}J_{3}=\{1,3\}, so a3=2a_{3}=2 selects p3=1p_{3}=1. The resulting tree is shown in Figure 1. Its left-child set is {3,4}=bl⁡(f)∖{1}\{3,4\}=\bl(f)\setminus\{1\}, and its maximal right chains recover the three kernel blocks.

1.3 The associated poset

We now order the synchronised tuples by simultaneous refinement of their kernel partitions. This order retains the subexceedant labellings and uses the common block-minimum set as a rank parameter.

Definition 1.4.

For 𝐟,𝐠∈𝒬n,ℓ\mathbf{f},\mathbf{g}\in\mathcal{Q}_{n,\ell}, define the strict order by

𝐟<𝐠⟺ker(fa) properly coarsens ker(ga)(a∈[ℓ]).\mathbf{f}<\mathbf{g}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\ker(f_{a})\text{ properly coarsens }\ker(g_{a})\quad(a\in[\ell]).

Adjoining equality gives the order ≤\leq. We use 𝒬n,ℓ\mathcal{Q}_{n,\ell} for both the poset and its underlying set.

Distinct tuples with the same tuple of kernels are incomparable. In particular, the order retains the subexceedant labellings of the blocks.

Proof of Theorem A(ii).

The defining relation is a partial order because proper refinement of set partitions is transitive. If 𝐟<𝐠\mathbf{f}<\mathbf{g}, then B⁡(𝐟)⊊B⁡(𝐠)B(\mathbf{f})\subsetneq B(\mathbf{g}): the minimum of each coarse block is the minimum of one of the fine blocks it contains.

Suppose that |B⁡(𝐠)|−|B⁡(𝐟)|≥2|B(\mathbf{g})|-|B(\mathbf{f})|\geq 2. We choose v∈B⁡(𝐠)∖B⁡(𝐟)v\in B(\mathbf{g})\setminus B(\mathbf{f}). In coordinate aa, let DaD_{a} be the block of ker⁡(ga)\ker(g_{a}) with minimum vv, and let CaC_{a} be the block of ker⁡(fa)\ker(f_{a}) containing it. We split CaC_{a} into DaD_{a} and Ca∖DaC_{a}\setminus D_{a}. The latter is nonempty and retains the minimum of CaC_{a}, since v∉B⁡(𝐟)v\notin B(\mathbf{f}). The resulting partition has block-minimum set B⁡(𝐟)∪{v}B(\mathbf{f})\cup\{v\} and lies strictly between the two original partitions. Labelling each of its blocks by its minimum gives a subexceedant function. Performing this operation in every coordinate therefore gives a tuple strictly between 𝐟\mathbf{f} and 𝐠\mathbf{g}, of rank one greater than 𝐟\mathbf{f}.

Covers are exactly the comparable pairs whose numbers of blocks differ by one. The one-block partition has the unique subexceedant labelling 11⋯111\cdots 1, and the discrete partition has the unique subexceedant labelling 12⋯n12\cdots n. This proves the assertions about rank and bounds. The rank enumeration follows from the enumeration of synchronised tuples by their number of blocks. ∎

2 A stability theorem for triangular recurrences

We prove Theorem B. After recalling stability preservers, we develop the path normalisation and finite multiplier lemmas used in the proof.

2.1 Stability preservers

A nonzero polynomial with real coefficients is real stable if it does not vanish when all its variables have positive imaginary part. For a univariate real polynomial, stability is equivalent to real-rootedness. We recall the standard stability preservers; see Srivastava [24, Theorem 2.7].

Proposition 2.1 (Stability preservers).

The following operations preserve real stability, provided the resulting polynomial is nonzero:

  1. 1.

    multiplication of real stable polynomials;

  2. 2.

    permutation of variables and substitution zi↦ai​ziz_{i}\mapsto a_{i}z_{i} with ai>0a_{i}>0;

  3. 3.

    identification of two or more variables;

  4. 4.

    specialisation of any variable to a real constant;

  5. 5.

    partial differentiation;

  6. 6.

    the substitution f(𝐳)↦zidif(z1,…,−1/zi,…,zm)f(\mathbf{z})\mapsto z_{i}^{d_{i}}f(z_{1},\ldots,-1/z_{i},\ldots,z_{m}), where di=degzi⁡fd_{i}=\deg_{z_{i}}f.

Only specialisation and differentiation can produce the zero polynomial from a nonzero stable input in this list.

We also use the homogenization theorem of Borcea, Brändén and Liggett [3, Theorem 4.5]: a polynomial with nonnegative coefficients is real stable if and only if its homogenization is real stable. In particular, for every integer D≥deg⁡fD\geq\deg f,

HD​(𝐳,y)=yD​f​(𝐳/y)H_{D}(\mathbf{z},y)=y^{D}f(\mathbf{z}/y) (2.1)

is real stable whenever ff is real stable and has nonnegative coefficients. Polarization also preserves stability [3, Corollary 4.7]: replacing yjy^{j} by ej​(y1,…,yD)/(Dj)e_{j}(y_{1},\ldots,y_{D})/\binom{D}{j}, where eje_{j} is the elementary symmetric polynomial, preserves stability for polynomials of degree at most DD in yy.

2.2 Weighted paths and multivariate refinements

We use the path interpretation in [22, Section 2 and Theorem 5]. Fix an initial vertex (k0,n0)(k_{0},n_{0}), and consider paths whose steps are N=(0,1)N=(0,1) and C=(1,1)C=(1,1), called north and cross steps, respectively. For the affine triangular recurrence

Tℓ​(n,k)=c​(n,k)ℓ​Tℓ​(n−1,k)+d​(n,k)ℓ​Tℓ​(n−1,k−1),T_{\ell}(n,k)=c(n,k)^{\ell}T_{\ell}(n-1,k)+d(n,k)^{\ell}T_{\ell}(n-1,k-1), (2.2)

where

c⁡(n,k)=α​n+β​k+γ,d⁡(n,k)=α′​n+β′​k+γ′,c(n,k)=\alpha n+\beta k+\gamma,\qquad d(n,k)=\alpha^{\prime}n+\beta^{\prime}k+\gamma^{\prime},

we take Tℓ​(n0,k0)=1T_{\ell}(n_{0},k_{0})=1 and zero entries outside k0≤k≤k0+n−n0k_{0}\leq k\leq k_{0}+n-n_{0}. A north step ending at (k,i)(k,i) has weight c⁡(i,k)c(i,k), and a cross step ending at (k,i)(k,i) has weight d⁡(i,k)d(i,k). Write wt⁡(p)\wt(p) for the product of these weights along a path pp, and C⁡(p)C(p) for the set of heights ii at which pp takes a cross step.

Let 𝒫n\mathcal{P}_{n} be the set of all paths from (k0,n0)(k_{0},n_{0}) to height nn. Define

ℱn,ℓ​(zn0+1,…,zn)=∑p∈𝒫nwt⁡(p)ℓ​∏i∈C⁡(p)zi,ℱn0,ℓ=1.\mathcal{F}_{n,\ell}(z_{n_{0}+1},\ldots,z_{n})=\sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}_{n}}\wt(p)^{\ell}\prod_{i\in C(p)}z_{i},\qquad\mathcal{F}_{n_{0},\ell}=1. (2.3)

Equivalently, a cross step ending at height ii receives the additional weight ziz_{i}, while every scalar step weight is raised to the power ℓ\ell. The path decomposition according to the last step gives

ℱn,ℓ​(t,…,t)=∑j=0n−n0Tℓ​(n,k0+j)​tj.\mathcal{F}_{n,\ell}(t,\ldots,t)=\sum_{j=0}^{n-n_{0}}T_{\ell}(n,k_{0}+j)t^{j}.

Thus the variables record the cross-step heights. For a prefix with jj cross steps, put

an​(j)=c⁡(n,k0+j),bn​(j)=d⁡(n,k0+j+1).a_{n}(j)=c(n,k_{0}+j),\qquad b_{n}(j)=d(n,k_{0}+j+1). (2.4)

These are the weights of its two outgoing steps. The following lemma, for which we do not include the proof, allows us the write the last step decomposition in terms of the operator Θ=∑i=n0+1n−1zi∂zi\Theta=\sum_{i=n_{0}+1}^{n-1}z_{i}\partial_{z_{i}}.

Lemma 2.2.

For f=∑j=0dfjf=\sum_{j=0}^{d}f_{j} with fjf_{j} homogeneous of degree jj in the variables zn0+1,…,zn−1z_{n_{0}+1},\dots,z_{n-1}, and Θ=∑i=n0+1n−1zi∂zi\Theta=\sum_{i=n_{0}+1}^{n-1}z_{i}\partial_{z_{i}}, we get

Θ⁡(f)=∑j=0dj​fj\Theta(f)=\sum_{j=0}^{d}jf_{j} (2.5)

Equivalently, for any rational function λ⁡(j)\lambda(j) in jj where the denominator does not vanish at j∈{0,1,…,d}j\in\{0,1,\dots,d\}, we have

λ⁡(Θ)=∑j=0dλ⁡(j)​fj.\lambda(\Theta)=\sum_{j=0}^{d}\lambda(j)f_{j}. (2.6)

So, the last-step decomposition can therefore be written as

ℱn,ℓ=[an​(Θ)ℓ+zn​bn​(Θ)ℓ]​ℱn−1,ℓ.\mathcal{F}_{n,\ell}=\bigl[a_{n}(\Theta)^{\ell}+z_{n}b_{n}(\Theta)^{\ell}\bigr]\mathcal{F}_{n-1,\ell}. (2.7)

Notice the shift by one in bn​(j)b_{n}(j) as a cross step increases the rank.

2.3 Finite multiplier sequences

The Pólya–Schur theorem characterizes diagonal operators that preserve real-rootedness [20]. We use its finite-degree form [8, Theorem 3.7]; see also [17, Theorem 4]. The following formulation for homogeneous components follows by homogenization and polarization.

Lemma 2.3.

Let η0,…,ηd≥0\eta_{0},\ldots,\eta_{d}\geq 0. For f=∑j=0dfjf=\sum_{j=0}^{d}f_{j}, with fjf_{j} homogeneous of degree jj, set

Mη​f=∑j=0dηj​fj,Jd​(η,t)=∑j=0d(dj)​ηj​tj.M_{\eta}f=\sum_{j=0}^{d}\eta_{j}f_{j},\qquad J_{d}(\eta;t)=\sum_{j=0}^{d}\binom{d}{j}\eta_{j}t^{j}.

where JdJ_{d} is the Jensen polynomial associated with the sequence ηj\eta_{j}. The operator MηM_{\eta} preserves real stability, allowing the zero polynomial, on polynomials with nonnegative coefficients and total degree at most dd, in any number of variables, if and only if Jd​(η,t)J_{d}(\eta;t) is zero or has only nonpositive real zeros.

Proof.

Necessity follows by applying the operator to (1+t)d(1+t)^{d}. For sufficiency, let ff be real stable with nonnegative coefficients, and first suppose that Jd​(η,t)=a​∏i=1d(t+ρi)J_{d}(\eta;t)=a\prod_{i=1}^{d}(t+\rho_{i}), where a>0a>0 and ρi≥0\rho_{i}\geq 0. We homogenize ff to degree dd and then polarize the homogenizing variable. The resulting stable polynomial is

H~​(𝐳,y1,…,yd)=∑j=0dfj​(𝐳)​ed−j​(y1,…,yd)(dj).\widetilde{H}(\mathbf{z},y_{1},\ldots,y_{d})=\sum_{j=0}^{d}f_{j}(\mathbf{z})\frac{e_{d-j}(y_{1},\ldots,y_{d})}{\binom{d}{j}}.

Comparing coefficients in the factorization of JdJ_{d} gives

Mη​f=a​H~​(𝐳,ρ1,…,ρd),M_{\eta}f=a\widetilde{H}(\mathbf{z},\rho_{1},\ldots,\rho_{d}),

which is stable or zero by real specialisation. If JdJ_{d} has degree q<dq<d, we can apply this argument to Jd​(η,t)​(1+ε​t)d−qJ_{d}(\eta;t)(1+\varepsilon t)^{d-q} and let ε\varepsilon tend to zero from above. Coefficient limits of stable polynomials are stable or zero, by Hurwitz’s theorem. The zero polynomial case is immediate. ∎

Lemma 2.4.

Let ff be a nonzero real stable polynomial with nonnegative coefficients, put Θ=∑izi∂zi\Theta=\sum_{i}z_{i}\partial_{z_{i}}, and let D≥deg⁡fD\geq\deg f be real. For every a>0a>0, the polynomial (Θ+a)​f(\Theta+a)f is real stable and has nonnegative coefficients. The same conclusion holds for (D−Θ)​f(D-\Theta)f unless this polynomial is zero.

Writing d=deg⁡fd=\deg f, the degree multipliers are j+aj+a and D−jD-j. For d≥1d\geq 1, their Jensen polynomials are

(1+t)d−1​(a+(a+d)​t),(1+t)d−1​(D+(D−d)​t),(1+t)^{d-1}\bigl(a+(a+d)t\bigr),\qquad(1+t)^{d-1}\bigl(D+(D-d)t\bigr),

respectively. We can now apply Lemma 2.3; the case d=0d=0 is immediate. The first operator has strictly positive degree multipliers and hence cannot annihilate ff. ∎

qj​Cj¯(A)j,qj(A)j,qj​Cj¯(0≤j≤d)q^{j}\frac{C^{\underline{j}}}{(A)_{j}},\qquad\frac{q^{j}}{(A)_{j}},\qquad q^{j}C^{\underline{j}}\qquad(0\leq j\leq d)

2.4 The affine stability theorem

We now impose hypotheses on (2.2). Assume

α,α′,β≥0,−α′≤β′≤0,\alpha,\alpha^{\prime},\beta\geq 0,\qquad-\alpha^{\prime}\leq\beta^{\prime}\leq 0, (2.10)

as in [22, Theorem 4], and require strictly positive weights on all accessible outgoing steps:

an(j)>0,bn(j)>0(n>n0, 0≤j≤n−n0−1).a_{n}(j)>0,\quad b_{n}(j)>0\qquad(n>n_{0},\ 0\leq j\leq n-n_{0}-1). (2.11)

The additional arithmetic conditions for our stability theorem are

αβ∈ℤ≥0if ​β>0,α′−β′∈ℤ≥1if ​β′<0.\frac{\alpha}{\beta}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}\quad\text{if }\beta>0,\qquad\frac{\alpha^{\prime}}{-\beta^{\prime}}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}\quad\text{if }\beta^{\prime}<0. (2.12)

For 0≤j≤n−n00\leq j\leq n-n_{0}, define

wn​(0)=1,wn​(j)=∏i=0j−1bn​(i)an​(i),𝒫n,ℓ=∑p∈𝒫nwt⁡(p)ℓwn​(|C⁡(p)|)ℓ​∏i∈C⁡(p)zi.w_{n}(0)=1,\qquad w_{n}(j)=\prod_{i=0}^{j-1}\frac{b_{n}(i)}{a_{n}(i)},\qquad\mathcal{P}_{n,\ell}=\sum_{p\in\mathcal{P}_{n}}\frac{\wt(p)^{\ell}}{w_{n}(|C(p)|)^{\ell}}\prod_{i\in C(p)}z_{i}. (2.13)

For n=n0n=n_{0}, set 𝒫n0,ℓ=1\mathcal{P}_{n_{0},\ell}=1.

Proof of Theorem B.

We set m=n−n0m=n-n_{0}. If β>0\beta>0 and β′<0\beta^{\prime}<0, we write

an​(j)=un​(j+An),bn​(j)=vn​(Cn−j),a_{n}(j)=u_{n}(j+A_{n}),\qquad b_{n}(j)=v_{n}(C_{n}-j),

3 Parametrised Eulerian polynomials

We prove Theorem C. Its stability assertion follows directly from the Eulerian specialisation in Table 1.

3.1 Real stability and real-rootedness

The binomial normalisation below is the multivariate form of Alexandersson’s univariate normalisation [1, Section 5]. Theorem C gives a stable refinement and strengthens the consecutive interlacing to strict interlacing. Recall that

Fn,ℓ(z2,…,zn)=∑e∈{0,1}n−1c(e)ℓ∏i:ei=1zi,F1,ℓ=1.F_{n,\ell}(z_{2},\ldots,z_{n})=\sum_{e\in\{0,1\}^{n-1}}c(e)^{\ell}\prod_{i:e_{i}=1}z_{i},\qquad F_{1,\ell}=1.

3.2 Strict interlacing

We next compare consecutive rows for a fixed parameter. The argument uses two intermediate polynomials: one shifts every root to the right and the other shifts every root to the left. Write θ=t​d/d​t\theta=t\,d/dt.

Lemma 3.1.

Let ff have positive leading coefficient and simple negative zeros ρ1<⋯<ρd<0\rho_{1}<\cdots<\rho_{d}<0, where d≥1d\geq 1, and let a>0a>0. Then (θ+a)​f(\theta+a)f has one simple zero in each of the intervals

(ρ1,ρ2),…,(ρd−1,ρd),(ρd,0),(\rho_{1},\rho_{2}),\ldots,(\rho_{d-1},\rho_{d}),(\rho_{d},0),

and (d+a−θ)​f(d+a-\theta)f has one simple zero in each of

(−∞,ρ1),(ρ1,ρ2),…,(ρd−1,ρd).(-\infty,\rho_{1}),(\rho_{1},\rho_{2}),\ldots,(\rho_{d-1},\rho_{d}).

Both transformed polynomials have degree dd and positive leading coefficient.

Proof.

At every zero of ff,

((θ+a)​f)​(ρi)=ρi​f′​(ρi),((d+a−θ)​f)​(ρi)=−ρi​f′​(ρi).((\theta+a)f)(\rho_{i})=\rho_{i}f^{\prime}(\rho_{i}),\qquad((d+a-\theta)f)(\rho_{i})=-\rho_{i}f^{\prime}(\rho_{i}).

The signs alternate with ii. The first polynomial is positive at zero, and the second has leading coefficient equal to aa times that of ff. These endpoint signs give a zero in each indicated interval. Each transformed polynomial has degree dd, so these dd distinct zeros account for all its zeros and are simple. ∎

For two real-rooted polynomials of the same degree, we say that their zeros weakly interlace if the ordered zeros alternate, allowing equalities. We use the following Hermite-Biehler criterion [3, Theorem 4.11]: if g⁡(t)+z​h​(t)g(t)+zh(t) is real stable and g,hg,h are nonzero real polynomials, then their zeros interlace.

Proof of Theorem C(ii).

The initial polynomial is A2,ℓ​(t)=1+tA_{2,\ell}(t)=1+t. Suppose that f=An,ℓf=A_{n,\ell} has simple negative zeros α1<⋯<αd\alpha_{1}<\cdots<\alpha_{d}, where d=n−1d=n-1. We set

is real stable. The preceding Hermite–Biehler criterion implies weak interlacing of UU and VV. The inequality v1<u1v_{1}<u_{1} fixes its orientation, giving

v1≤u1≤v2≤u2≤⋯≤vd≤ud.v_{1}\leq u_{1}\leq v_{2}\leq u_{2}\leq\cdots\leq v_{d}\leq u_{d}. (3.8)

ui−1≤vi<αi<ui≤vi+1,u_{i-1}\leq v_{i}<\alpha_{i}<u_{i}\leq v_{i+1},

(−∞,α1),(α1,α2),…,(αd−1,αd),(αd,0).(-\infty,\alpha_{1}),\quad(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}),\ldots,(\alpha_{d-1},\alpha_{d}),\quad(\alpha_{d},0).

Proof of Theorem C(iii).

The case n=1n=1 is immediate. For n≥2n\geq 2, we set q=An+1,ℓq=A_{n+1,\ell} and f=An,ℓf=A_{n,\ell}, and write α1<⋯<αn−1\alpha_{1}<\cdots<\alpha_{n-1} for the zeros of ff. Both are monic, and strict interlacing gives the partial-fraction expansion

q⁡(t)f⁡(t)=t+b−∑i=1n−1cit−αi,ci=−q⁡(αi)f′​(αi)>0.\frac{q(t)}{f(t)}=t+b-\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\frac{c_{i}}{t-\alpha_{i}},\qquad c_{i}=-\frac{q(\alpha_{i})}{f^{\prime}(\alpha_{i})}>0.

This ratio has positive imaginary part in the upper half-plane, so q⁡(t)+z​f​(t)q(t)+zf(t) cannot vanish when both tt and zz are in that half-plane. On each real interval between consecutive poles, including the two unbounded intervals, its derivative is

1+∑i=1n−1ci(t−αi)2>0,1+\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\frac{c_{i}}{(t-\alpha_{i})^{2}}>0,

and its range is all of ℝ\mathbb{R}. Thus q/f=−sq/f=-s has precisely one simple solution in each interval. Only the rightmost interval intersects [0,∞)[0,\infty), and q⁡(0)/f⁡(0)=1q(0)/f(0)=1 determines the asserted sign of its solution. ∎

3.3 Gamma coefficients and the Strong Rayleigh property

Theorem C(i) recovers the known gamma-positivity of An,ℓA_{n,\ell}. Indeed, Proposition 1.2 gives palindromicity and nonnegative coefficients, so Brändén’s criterion [5, Remark 3.1] gives nonnegative coefficients in (I.1). They are integers by successive coefficient comparison, since tj​(1+t)n−1−2​jt^{j}(1+t)^{n-1-2j} has lowest term tjt^{j} with coefficient 11. The stronger real-rootedness of Γn,ℓ\Gamma_{n,\ell} is included in Alexandersson’s theorem [1, Theorem 5.1]. Newton’s inequalities imply log-concavity and unimodality of the coefficients of An,ℓA_{n,\ell}; see [5, Section 1].

In probabilistic terms, the stable polynomial Fn,ℓF_{n,\ell} gives the strongly Rayleigh measure

μn,ℓ​(S)=c​(𝟏S)ℓAn,ℓ​(1)(S⊆{2,…,n}).\mu_{n,\ell}(S)=\frac{c(\mathbf{1}_{S})^{\ell}}{A_{n,\ell}(1)}\qquad(S\subseteq\{2,\ldots,n\}).

Here 𝟏S\mathbf{1}_{S} is the binary word with ones in the positions of SS. This is the distribution of the common block-minimum set, with 11 removed, under the uniform measure on 𝒬n,ℓ\mathcal{Q}_{n,\ell}.

4 Combinatorial interpretations of the gamma coefficients

We prove Theorem D by extending unary flips on a single increasing binary tree (the Foata-Strehl group action) to synchronised flips on pairs.

4.1 Unary flips for a single tree

We first recall the tree form of the modified Foata–Strehl action; see [11, 4, 19]. A vertex with two children is binary, and a vertex with exactly one child is unary. For v∈[n]v\in[n], define ϕv​(T)\phi_{v}(T) by moving the unique child subtree of vv to the opposite side when vv is unary, and by fixing TT otherwise. The parent relations do not change. Therefore the unary vertices remain the same, each ϕv\phi_{v} is an involution, and the maps ϕv\phi_{v} commute. They define an action of (ℤ/2​ℤ)n(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^{n} on 𝒯n\mathcal{T}_{n}.

Proposition 4.1.

An orbit whose trees have bb binary vertices and uu unary vertices has enumerator

tb​(1+t)u=tb​(1+t)n−1−2​b.t^{b}(1+t)^{u}=t^{b}(1+t)^{n-1-2b}.

Consequently, γn,1,k\gamma_{n,1,k} counts increasing plane binary trees with kk binary vertices and with every unary child on the right.

Proof.

Within an orbit, the orientation of each unary edge can be chosen independently, while the left and right children at binary vertices are fixed. Each binary vertex contributes one left child. Each unary edge contributes either zero or one left child, giving the factor 1+t1+t. Counting edges gives 2​b+u=n−12b+u=n-1. Every orbit contains a unique tree in which all unary children are on the right, and its number of left children is bb. Summing the orbit enumerators proves the gamma-coefficient interpretation. ∎

4.2 Sibling graphs and synchronised flips

For 𝐓∈𝒯n,ℓ\mathbf{T}\in\mathcal{T}_{n,\ell}, its sibling graph G⁡(𝐓)G(\mathbf{T}) is the simple graph on {2,…,n}\{2,\ldots,n\} with an edge {i,j}\{i,j\} whenever ii and jj are siblings in at least one coordinate tree. Each tree contributes a matching to this graph. Siblings have opposite left–right status, so G⁡(𝐓)G(\mathbf{T}) is bipartite with bipartition

L⁡(𝐓)⊔({2,…,n}∖L⁡(𝐓)).L(\mathbf{T})\ \sqcup\ \bigl(\{2,\ldots,n\}\setminus L(\mathbf{T})\bigr).

The graph records all restrictions on synchronised orientations. To make this precise, let 𝒰n,ℓ\mathcal{U}_{n,\ell} be the set of ordered ℓ\ell-tuples of increasing rooted trees on [n][n] having at most two children at each vertex, with no left–right order. Define G⁡(𝐔)G(\mathbf{U}) by the same sibling rule. For a connected bipartite component CC, write aC,bCa_{C},b_{C} for its two part sizes; for an isolated vertex, these sizes are 00 and 11.

Proposition 4.2.

A tuple 𝐔∈𝒰n,ℓ\mathbf{U}\in\mathcal{U}_{n,\ell} admits a synchronised plane orientation if and only if G⁡(𝐔)G(\mathbf{U}) is bipartite. Moreover,

An,ℓ​(t)=∑𝐔∈𝒰n,ℓG⁡(𝐔)​ bipartite∏C∈Comp⁡(G⁡(𝐔))(taC+tbC).A_{n,\ell}(t)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{U}\in\mathcal{U}_{n,\ell}\\ G(\mathbf{U})\text{ bipartite}\end{subarray}}\prod_{C\in\operatorname{Comp}(G(\mathbf{U}))}(t^{a_{C}}+t^{b_{C}}). (4.1)
Proof.

We assign to each nonroot label its common left–right status in all coordinates. This assignment gives a valid plane orientation precisely when siblings receive opposite statuses, that is, when it is a proper two-colouring of G⁡(𝐔)G(\mathbf{U}). Each connected bipartite component has exactly two such colourings, contributing taCt^{a_{C}} and tbCt^{b_{C}}. Choices on different components are independent. Summing over 𝐔\mathbf{U} proves the identity. ∎

For a connected component CC of G⁡(𝐓)G(\mathbf{T}), define its component flip by reversing the left–right status of every label in CC, simultaneously in every coordinate. More explicitly, when a label in CC has a sibling in a given tree, that sibling also belongs to CC, and the two child subtrees are exchanged. When it has no sibling, its subtree is moved to the other side of its parent. This definition includes unary edges. Parent relations and labels do not change, so the sibling graph and its components remain unchanged. The flip is an involution on synchronised tuples.

We now specialise to ℓ=2\ell=2.

Lemma 4.3.

Every component of G⁡(𝐓)G(\mathbf{T}) for 𝐓∈𝒯n,2\mathbf{T}\in\mathcal{T}_{n,2} is a path or an even cycle. An odd component of size 2​a+12a+1 has bipartition sizes a,a+1a,a+1, and an even component of size 2​b2b has bipartition sizes b,bb,b.

Proof.

The graph is bipartite and is the union of two matchings, so its maximum degree is at most two. Its components are therefore paths or even cycles. Alternating the two parts along a path or cycle gives the claimed sizes. ∎

For each i∈{2,…,n}i\in\{2,\ldots,n\}, define a map τi\tau_{i} on the whole set 𝒯n,2\mathcal{T}_{n,2} as follows: if ii is the smallest label of an odd component of G⁡(𝐓)G(\mathbf{T}), flip that component; otherwise fix 𝐓\mathbf{T}. In particular, even components are never flipped. We call this the modified synchronised Foata–Strehl action.

Proof of Theorem D(i): the action and orbit enumerator.

Component flips preserve the sibling graph, including its component minima. Thus applying τi\tau_{i} twice restores the original tuple. Two distinct nontrivial generators change the statuses of disjoint sets of labels and hence commute. Their actions remain independent even when the corresponding child subtrees are nested, because the underlying parent relations are fixed.

Let ss be the number of odd components and put k=∑C∈Comp⁡(G⁡(𝐓))⌊|C|/2⌋k=\sum_{C\in\Comp(G(\mathbf{T}))}\lfloor|C|/2\rfloor. An odd component of size 2​a+12a+1 contributes ta+ta+1t^{a}+t^{a+1} to the orbit enumerator. An even component of size 2​b2b retains its orientation and contributes tbt^{b}. By Lemma 4.3, multiplication over components gives tk​(1+t)st^{k}(1+t)^{s}. Finally, summing the component sizes gives n−1=2​k+sn-1=2k+s. ∎

Call 𝐓∈𝒯n,2\mathbf{T}\in\mathcal{T}_{n,2} reduced if every odd component CC satisfies

|C∩L⁡(𝐓)|=|C|−12.|C\cap L(\mathbf{T})|=\frac{|C|-1}{2}.

There is no additional restriction on even components.

Proof of Theorem D(i): the reduced representatives.

Each odd component has a unique orientation with its smaller part on the left. The modified action chooses these orientations independently and fixes all even-component orientations. Every orbit therefore has exactly one reduced pair. Its number of common left-child labels is the exponent kk in (I.4). Summing that identity over all orbits proves (I.1) for ℓ=2\ell=2, with the asserted counting interpretation. A tree without left children is the unique right chain on [n][n], so there is exactly one reduced pair with no left children. ∎

The gamma-positivity of An,2A_{n,2} was proved algebraically by Shankar [22, Proposition 27]. Theorem D gives a group action and a combinatorial interpretation of its gamma coefficients. When there is only one coordinate tree, the sibling graph consists of isolated vertices and single edges. Its odd components are exactly the labels of unary children, so the same construction reduces to the unary action above.

Example 4.4.

Take the pair (T1,T2)(T_{1},T_{2}) in Figure 2, with common left-child set {2}\{2\}. Its sibling graph consists of the path −−43\!-\!2\!-\!4 and the isolated vertex 55. Thus the two active generators are τ2\tau_{2}, which flips C={2,3,4}C=\{2,3,4\}, and τ5\tau_{5}, which flips D={5}D=\{5\}. The original pair is reduced: on each odd component, the left vertices occupy the smaller colour class.

Table 2 gives the four orbit elements through their inverse images under Φ5\Phi_{5} in each coordinate. In every row the common block-minimum set is {1}∪L\{1\}\cup L. The orbit enumerator is

t+2​t2+t3=t​(1+t)2,t+2t^{2}+t^{3}=t(1+t)^{2},

so this orbit contributes one to γ5,2,1\gamma_{5,2,1}.

4.3 A recurrence for the gamma coefficients

Expanding the differential recurrence of Shankar [22, Proposition 26] in the gamma basis gives the two-term recurrence in Theorem D(ii) for the reduced-pair numbers. We give the calculation in its univariate form.

Proof of Theorem D(ii).

Let θ=t​d/d​t\theta=t\,d/dt. The defining recurrence for the coefficients of An,2A_{n,2} gives

An,2=((θ+1)2+t​(n−1−θ)2)​An−1,2.A_{n,2}=\bigl((\theta+1)^{2}+t(n-1-\theta)^{2}\bigr)A_{n-1,2}.

((θ+1)2+t​(n−1−θ)2)​tj​(1+t)q\displaystyle\bigl((\theta+1)^{2}+t(n-1-\theta)^{2}\bigr)t^{j}(1+t)^{q}
=(j+1)2​tj​(1+t)q+1+q⁡(q+4​j+5)​tj+1​(1+t)q−1,\displaystyle\qquad=(j+1)^{2}t^{j}(1+t)^{q+1}+q(q+4j+5)t^{j+1}(1+t)^{q-1}, (4.2)

5 PECKness and combinatorial 𝔰​𝔩2\mathfrak{sl}_{2} actions

We prove Theorem E and discuss Conjecture 1.

We return to the posets defined in Section 1.3. The kernel-preserving tree bijection makes it possible to construct linear operators supported on their cover relations when ℓ=1\ell=1. We first recall the representation-theoretic mechanism that turns these operators into a proof of the strong Sperner property.

5.1 The combinatorial 𝔰​𝔩2\mathfrak{sl}_{2} mechanism

Let PkP_{k} denote the set of elements of rank kk in a finite graded poset PP. A finite graded poset PP of rank NN is rank-symmetric if |Pk|=|PN−k||P_{k}|=|P_{N-k}| for every kk, and rank-unimodal if its rank sizes are unimodal. It is strongly Sperner if, for every 1≤s≤N+11\leq s\leq N+1, the largest union of ss antichains has size equal to the sum of its ss largest rank sizes. A poset having all three properties is called a PECK poset.

Let Vk=ℂ​PkV_{k}=\mathbb{C}P_{k} be the vector space with basis the elements of PkP_{k}, and put V=⨁k=0NVkV=\bigoplus_{k=0}^{N}V_{k}. A linear map E:V→VE:V\to V is order-raising if

E​x∈span⁡{y∈P:y⋗x}(x∈P).Ex\in\operatorname{span}\{y\in P:y\gtrdot x\}\qquad(x\in P).

The linear-algebraic approach to Sperner theory replaces matchings between ranks by order-raising maps of full rank. Stanley’s textbook [26, Chapter 4] explains this approach through the up and down operators on Boolean lattices. For strong Sperner properties, we use the following criterion.

Theorem 5.1 ([25, Lemma 1.1]).

A finite graded poset PP of rank NN is PECK if and only if there is an order-raising map EE such that

EN−2​k:Vk⟶VN−kis an isomorphism for ​0≤k≤⌊N/2⌋.E^{N-2k}:V_{k}\longrightarrow V_{N-k}\quad\text{is an isomorphism for }0\leq k\leq\lfloor N/2\rfloor. (5.1)

The Lie algebra 𝔰​𝔩2​(ℂ)\mathfrak{sl}_{2}(\mathbb{C}) has generators e,f,he,f,h with [h,e]=2​e[h,e]=2e, [h,f]=−2​f[h,f]=-2f, and [e,f]=h[e,f]=h, where [X,Y]=X​Y−Y​X[X,Y]=XY-YX. Its finite-dimensional representations are direct sums of irreducible modules; see [15, Sections 6–7]. For each integer d≥0d\geq 0, the irreducible module of highest weight dd has a basis v0,…,vdv_{0},\ldots,v_{d} in which

h​vi=(2​i−d)​vi,e​vi=(d−i)​vi+1,f​vi=i​vi−1,hv_{i}=(2i-d)v_{i},\qquad ev_{i}=(d-i)v_{i+1},\qquad fv_{i}=iv_{i-1}, (5.2)

with the terms outside the index range interpreted as zero. Thus the weights form a string symmetric about zero, and powers of ee identify opposite weight spaces. Assigning weight 2​k−N2k-N to rank kk turns these identifications into the isomorphisms in (5.1). See, for example, Proctor [21] and Gaetz–Gao [12]. The following lemma gives another sufficient condition for PECKness. We include the proof here to keep the article self-contained.

Lemma 5.2.

Suppose that EE is order-raising, that F⁡(Vk)⊆Vk−1F(V_{k})\subseteq V_{k-1}, and that H|Vk=(2​k−N)​IH|_{V_{k}}=(2k-N)I. If

[H,E]=2​E,[H,F]=−2​F,[E,F]=H,[H,E]=2E,\qquad[H,F]=-2F,\qquad[E,F]=H, (5.3)

then PP is PECK.

Proof.

The relations give an 𝔰​𝔩2\mathfrak{sl}_{2}-representation on VV. In each irreducible summand, (5.2) shows that EmE^{m} identifies the weight −m-m and weight mm spaces for every integer m≥0m\geq 0; both spaces are zero when these weights do not occur. Taking direct sums and setting m=N−2​km=N-2k gives (5.1), so Theorem 5.1 applies. ∎

5.2 Linear operators for ℓ=1\ell=1

We use the bijection Φn\Phi_{n} of Theorem A to identify the basis of ℂ​𝒬n,1\mathbb{C}\mathcal{Q}_{n,1} with the increasing binary trees in 𝒯n\mathcal{T}_{n}. The rank of a tree is its number of left edges, and its maximal right chains give the blocks of the corresponding kernel.

For a tree TT, let Ru​(T)R_{u}(T), respectively Lu​(T)L_{u}(T), be the set of labels of right, respectively left, children whose parents have exactly one child. If i∈Ru​(T)∪Lu​(T)i\in R_{u}(T)\cup L_{u}(T), write σi​T\sigma_{i}T for the tree obtained by moving the subtree rooted at ii to the opposite child slot of its parent. Define

E​T=∑i∈Ru​(T)σi​T,F​T=∑i∈Lu​(T)σi​T,H​T=(2​ρ​(T)−n+1)​T.ET=\sum_{i\in R_{u}(T)}\sigma_{i}T,\qquad FT=\sum_{i\in L_{u}(T)}\sigma_{i}T,\qquad HT=(2\rho(T)-n+1)T. (5.4)
Proof of Theorem E: the operators and PECKness.

Moving a unary right edge to the left splits one maximal right chain into two and leaves the other right chains unchanged. By the kernel-preserving property of Φn\Phi_{n}, this splits one kernel block. Theorem A(ii) shows that every summand of E​TET is an upper cover of TT. Reversing the move merges two right chains, so every summand of F​TFT is a lower cover.

To verify the commutators, we fix the parent relations of a tree and the left–right order at every vertex having two children, and forget only the orientations at vertices having one child. We call the resulting object a skeleton. Suppose that it has bb vertices with two children and uu unary edges. Counting edges gives

n−1=2​b+u.n-1=2b+u.

We index the unary edges by [u][u]. The orientations of this skeleton have basis eSe_{S}, S⊆[u]S\subseteq[u], where SS records the edges oriented to the left. These basis vectors have rank b+|S|b+|S|, and the operators restrict to

E​eS\displaystyle Ee_{S} =∑i∉SeS∪{i},\displaystyle=\sum_{i\notin S}e_{S\cup\{i\}}, F​eS\displaystyle Fe_{S} =∑i∈SeS∖{i},\displaystyle=\sum_{i\in S}e_{S\setminus\{i\}}, H​eS\displaystyle He_{S} =(2​|S|−u)​eS.\displaystyle=(2|S|-u)e_{S}. (5.5)

The first two relations in (5.3) follow because EE raises |S||S| by one and FF lowers it by one. In (E​F−F​E)​eS(EF-FE)e_{S}, the terms changing two distinct edges cancel in pairs. The coefficient of eSe_{S} is |S|−(u−|S|)=2​|S|−u|S|-(u-|S|)=2|S|-u, proving [E,F]=H[E,F]=H.

Each skeleton spans an invariant subspace, and the skeleton classes partition the tree basis. The relations therefore hold on the whole space. We can now apply Lemma 5.2 to obtain PECKness. ∎

The same construction also gives a partition into symmetric Boolean subposets. A symmetric Boolean decomposition of a graded poset of rank NN is a partition into Boolean subposets whose ranks agree with the ambient ranks up to a shift and whose minimum and maximum ranks sum to NN. A symmetric chain decomposition is a partition into saturated chains with the same condition on their endpoint ranks.

Proof of Theorem E: the symmetric decompositions.

We fix a skeleton with bb binary vertices and uu unary edges. The orientations of a fixed skeleton form a Boolean subposet, with S⊆S′S\subseteq S^{\prime} corresponding to changing unary right edges to left edges. Conversely, comparability of two orientations implies inclusion of their left-child label sets, hence inclusion of the corresponding subsets of unary edges. Thus the induced order is Boolean. Its ranks range from bb to b+ub+u, and 2​b+u=n−12b+u=n-1 makes it symmetric. These subposets partition 𝒬n,1\mathcal{Q}_{n,1}.

For completeness, a symmetric chain decomposition of a Boolean lattice can be constructed inductively. We start with the one-element lattice ℬ0\mathcal{B}_{0}. Given a symmetric chain x0<⋯<xmx_{0}<\cdots<x_{m} in ℬu\mathcal{B}_{u}, we partition its product with {0,1}\{0,1\} into

(x0,0)<⋯<(xm,0)<(xm,1),(x0,1)<⋯<(xm−1,1),(x_{0},0)<\cdots<(x_{m},0)<(x_{m},1),\qquad(x_{0},1)<\cdots<(x_{m-1},1),

omitting the second chain if m=0m=0. Both chains are saturated and symmetric in ℬu+1\mathcal{B}_{u+1}. Applying this to every chain and then to each skeleton class proves the second assertion. ∎

Example 5.3.

The poset 𝒬4,1\mathcal{Q}_{4,1} has rank sizes (1,11,11,1)(1,11,11,1). A symmetric chain decomposition consists of the chain

1111⋖1114⋖1134⋖12341111\lessdot 1114\lessdot 1134\lessdot 1234

and the following ten chains:

1212⋖12131211⋖12141221⋖12311131⋖12321222⋖12241133⋖12331113⋖12231121⋖11231122⋖11241112⋖1132.\begin{array}[]{@{}c@{\qquad}c@{}}1212\lessdot 1213&1211\lessdot 1214\\[2.0pt] 1221\lessdot 1231&1131\lessdot 1232\\[2.0pt] 1222\lessdot 1224&1133\lessdot 1233\\[2.0pt] 1113\lessdot 1223&1121\lessdot 1123\\[2.0pt] 1122\lessdot 1124&1112\lessdot 1132.\end{array}

The first chain has endpoint ranks 00 and 33; every other chain has endpoint ranks 11 and 22. All 2424 subexceedant functions occur exactly once. Each step splits one kernel block. For example, 1113⋖12231113\lessdot 1223 splits {1,2,3}|{4}\{1,2,3\}\mid\{4\} into {1}​∣{2,3}∣​{4}\{1\}\mid\{2,3\}\mid\{4\}.

5.3 The PECK conjecture for higher parameters

The rank polynomial An,ℓ​(t)A_{n,\ell}(t) is palindromic by Proposition 1.2 and real-rooted by Theorem C(i). Consequently, 𝒬n,ℓ\mathcal{Q}_{n,\ell} is rank-symmetric and rank-unimodal for every n,ℓn,\ell. The remaining PECK condition concerns its order.

Conjecture 1 asserts that 𝒬n,ℓ\mathcal{Q}_{n,\ell} is PECK for every ℓ>1\ell>1.

Equivalently, it remains to prove that these posets are strongly Sperner. The component flips used in the ℓ=2\ell=2 group action do not directly give the required order-raising operators. Flipping an odd path with at least three vertices replaces one nonempty set of left-child labels by another disjoint nonempty set. The two block-minimum sets are then incomparable by inclusion, so the two tuples are incomparable in 𝒬n,2\mathcal{Q}_{n,2}.

There is computational evidence for the stronger assertion that 𝒬n,ℓ\mathcal{Q}_{n,\ell} admits a symmetric chain decomposition. If PkP_{k} and Pk+1P_{k+1} are consecutive ranks and N⁡(X)N(X) is the set of upper neighbours of X⊆PkX\subseteq P_{k}, the normalised matching property is

|N⁡(X)||Pk+1|≥|X||Pk|(X⊆Pk).\frac{|N(X)|}{|P_{k+1}|}\geq\frac{|X|}{|P_{k}|}\qquad(X\subseteq P_{k}). (5.6)

A rank-symmetric, rank-unimodal poset satisfying this property at every pair of consecutive ranks admits a symmetric chain decomposition [13]. We have verified (5.6) throughout the following ranges:

ℓ234n1≤n≤81≤n≤71≤n≤6.\begin{array}[]{c|ccc}\ell&2&3&4\\ \hline\cr n&1\leq n\leq 8&1\leq n\leq 7&1\leq n\leq 6.\end{array}

For ℓ=2\ell=2, explicit symmetric chain decompositions have also been constructed and checked through n=7n=7.

6 Extensions to Stirling permutations

We prove Theorems F and G.

The same normalisation applies to descent numbers of Stirling permutations. We distinguish the multiplicity mm of each letter from the synchronisation parameter ℓ\ell. Ordinary Stirling permutations correspond to m=2m=2, whereas m=1m=1 gives ordinary permutations.

6.1 Descent histories and stability

An mm-Stirling permutation of order nn is a permutation of {1m,…,nm}\{1^{m},\ldots,n^{m}\} in which no smaller letter occurs between two consecutive occurrences of a letter. We count only internal descents:

d⁡(σ)=|{i:1≤i⁡<m​n,σi>​σi+1}|.d(\sigma)=|\{i:1\leq i<mn,\ \sigma_{i}>\sigma_{i+1}\}|.

Thus the customary mandatory descent to a terminal zero is omitted. If σ[i]\sigma^{[i]} is obtained by deleting all letters greater than ii, put ei=d⁡(σ[i])−d⁡(σ[i−1])e_{i}=d(\sigma^{[i]})-d(\sigma^{[i-1]}) for 2≤i≤n2\leq i\leq n. The largest letter is inserted as one consecutive block, so eie_{i} is either zero or one. We call (e2,…,en)(e_{2},\ldots,e_{n}) its descent history.

For a history ee, set ki=e2+⋯+ei−1k_{i}=e_{2}+\cdots+e_{i-1} and

cm​(e)=∏i=2n{ki+1,ei=0,m⁡(i−1)−ki,ei=1.c_{m}(e)=\prod_{i=2}^{n}\begin{cases}k_{i}+1,&e_{i}=0,\\ m(i-1)-k_{i},&e_{i}=1.\end{cases} (6.1)

Indeed, a word on [i−1][i-1] with kik_{i} descents has ki+1k_{i}+1 descent-preserving insertion gaps: its descent gaps and its final gap. The remaining m⁡(i−1)−kim(i-1)-k_{i} gaps create a descent. Consequently, cm​(e)c_{m}(e) counts the words with history ee.

An ordered ℓ\ell-tuple is synchronised when its coordinates have the same descent history. Define

Fn,ℓ(m)(𝐳)=∑e∈{0,1}n−1cm(e)ℓ∏i:ei=1zi,Sn,ℓ(m)(t)=Fn,ℓ(m)(t,…,t).F^{(m)}_{n,\ell}(\mathbf{z})=\sum_{e\in\{0,1\}^{n-1}}c_{m}(e)^{\ell}\prod_{i:e_{i}=1}z_{i},\qquad S^{(m)}_{n,\ell}(t)=F^{(m)}_{n,\ell}(t,\ldots,t). (6.2)

Writing Sℓ(m)​(n,k)=[tk]​Sn,ℓ(m)​(t)S^{(m)}_{\ell}(n,k)=[t^{k}]S^{(m)}_{n,\ell}(t) gives

Sℓ(m)​(n,k)=(k+1)ℓ​Sℓ(m)​(n−1,k)+(m⁡(n−1)−k+1)ℓ​Sℓ(m)​(n−1,k−1),S^{(m)}_{\ell}(n,k)=(k+1)^{\ell}S^{(m)}_{\ell}(n-1,k)+(m(n-1)-k+1)^{\ell}S^{(m)}_{\ell}(n-1,k-1), (6.3)

with Sℓ(m)​(1,0)=1S^{(m)}_{\ell}(1,0)=1 and zero entries outside 0≤k≤n−10\leq k\leq n-1. For m=1m=1, these are the parametrised Eulerian polynomials.

Proof of Theorem F(i).

Stability follows from Theorem B and the mm-Stirling row of Table 1; its balancing weights are wn​(k)=(m⁡(n−1)k)w_{n}(k)=\binom{m(n-1)}{k}.

For strict interlacing, the initial nonconstant polynomial is S2,ℓ(m)=1+mℓ​tS^{(m)}_{2,\ell}=1+m^{\ell}t. Suppose that f=Sn,ℓ(m)f=S^{(m)}_{n,\ell} has simple negative zeros α1<⋯<αd\alpha_{1}<\cdots<\alpha_{d}, where d=n−1d=n-1, and put

U=(θ+1)ℓ​f,V=(m​n−θ)ℓ​f,θ=t​dd​t.U=(\theta+1)^{\ell}f,\qquad V=(mn-\theta)^{\ell}f,\qquad\theta=t\frac{d}{dt}.

Then Sn+1,ℓ(m)=U+t​VS^{(m)}_{n+1,\ell}=U+tV. Since m​n>dmn>d, Lemma 3.1, applied successively, gives simple negative zeros uiu_{i} and viv_{i} satisfying vi<αi<uiv_{i}<\alpha_{i}<u_{i}. Specializing the old variables of Fn+1,ℓ(m)F^{(m)}_{n+1,\ell} to tt gives the stable polynomial U⁡(t)+z​V​(t)U(t)+zV(t). Hence its coefficient polynomials weakly interlace, in the order

v1≤u1≤v2≤u2≤⋯≤vd≤ud.v_{1}\leq u_{1}\leq v_{2}\leq u_{2}\leq\cdots\leq v_{d}\leq u_{d}.

Both leading coefficients are positive. It follows that sgn⁡U⁡(αi)=(−1)d−i+1\operatorname{sgn}U(\alpha_{i})=(-1)^{d-i+1} and sgn⁡V⁡(αi)=(−1)d−i\operatorname{sgn}V(\alpha_{i})=(-1)^{d-i}. Since αi<0\alpha_{i}<0, the two summands of U⁡(αi)+αi​V​(αi)U(\alpha_{i})+\alpha_{i}V(\alpha_{i}) have the same nonzero sign. Together with the positive constant and leading coefficients, this places one zero in each of

(−∞,α1),(αi,αi+1)​(1≤i<d),(αd,0).(-\infty,\alpha_{1}),\quad(\alpha_{i},\alpha_{i+1})\ (1\leq i<d),\quad(\alpha_{d},0).

Degree counting proves simplicity and strict interlacing. The Strong Rayleigh, log-concavity, and unimodality assertions follow from stability and its univariate specialisation, as in Section 3.

The proof of Theorem C(iii) also shows that Sn+1,ℓ(m)​(t)+z​Sn,ℓ(m)​(t)S^{(m)}_{n+1,\ell}(t)+zS^{(m)}_{n,\ell}(t) is real stable. The only change is that the linear part of the quotient of consecutive rows has slope equal to the positive ratio of their leading coefficients. Every real combination Sn+1,ℓ(m)+s​Sn,ℓ(m)S^{(m)}_{n+1,\ell}+sS^{(m)}_{n,\ell} therefore has simple real zeros; all are negative for s>−1s>-1, one is zero for s=−1s=-1, and exactly one is positive for s<−1s<-1. ∎

At ℓ=1\ell=1, real-rootedness belongs to the classical theory; see Brenti [6] and Bóna [2]. Haglund–Visontai [14] proved stability for multivariate refinements marking ascent, descent, and plateau values. The polynomial (6.2) records insertion histories, which differ from the final descent-top sets.

Remark 6.1.

The proof also permits positive multiplicities m1,…,mnm_{1},\ldots,m_{n}. We put C1=0C_{1}=0 and Ci=m1+⋯+mi−1C_{i}=m_{1}+\cdots+m_{i-1} for i≥2i\geq 2 and replace m⁡(i−1)m(i-1) by CiC_{i} in (6.1). The balancing weights are (Cnk)\binom{C_{n}}{k}, and the normalised recurrence becomes

Pn,ℓC=(1+zn)​[(Θ+1)​∏j=Cn−1+1Cnj−Θj]ℓ​Pn−1,ℓC.P_{n,\ell}^{C}=(1+z_{n})\left[(\Theta+1)\prod_{j=C_{n-1}+1}^{C_{n}}\frac{j-\Theta}{j}\right]^{\ell}P_{n-1,\ell}^{C}.

Every displayed factor preserves stability by Lemma 2.4, and the binomial multiplier restores the unnormalized polynomial. Since Cn+1≥nC_{n+1}\geq n, the interlacing proof is unchanged. Thus all the conclusions of Theorem F(i) hold for a fixed infinite sequence of positive multiplicities.

6.2 Trees and the kernel order

For constant multiplicity mm, replace subexceedant functions by maps f:[n]→[m⁡(n−1)+1]f:[n]\to[m(n-1)+1] satisfying f⁡(i)≤m⁡(i−1)+1f(i)\leq m(i-1)+1. Their kernels and block-leader sets are defined as before. Let ℛn,ℓ(m)\mathcal{R}^{(m)}_{n,\ell} be their synchronised ℓ\ell-tuples, ordered by proper kernel refinement in every coordinate, as in Definition 1.4.

Proof of Theorem F(ii).

We number the child slots 0,…,m0,\ldots,m, with mm the rightmost slot. We fix a partition with block minima 1=b1<⋯<bs1=b_{1}<\cdots<b_{s}. After choosing the distinct images of its first j−1j-1 blocks, the number of available images for the next block is

m⁡(bj−1)+1−(j−1)=m⁡(bj−1)−j+2.m(b_{j}-1)+1-(j-1)=m(b_{j}-1)-j+2.

We form the prescribed increasing rightmost chains and attach their roots bjb_{j}, for j≥2j\geq 2, in increasing order to unused nonrightmost slots at vertices smaller than bjb_{j}. There are m⁡(bj−1)m(b_{j}-1) such slots before attachments and j−2j-2 have already been used. We match available images, in increasing order, with available slots, ordered first by parent label and then by slot number. The counts agree. All edges increase labels, and the construction is invertible by recovering the rightmost chains and reversing these choices.

The Gessel correspondence reads a vertex aa with subtrees T0,…,TmT_{0},\ldots,T_{m} as

W(T)=W(T0)aW(T1)a⋯aW(Tm),W(∅)=∅;W(T)=W(T_{0})\,a\,W(T_{1})\,a\,\cdots\,a\,W(T_{m}),\qquad W(\varnothing)=\varnothing;

see [16, Theorems 1–2]. The labels in a nonempty TjT_{j}, j<mj<m, are larger than aa, so the last letter of W⁡(Tj)W(T_{j}) followed by aa contributes one descent. The intervening transitions contribute no additional descents. Induction therefore identifies the number of internal descents with the number of nonrightmost edges. Deleting the largest vertex simply removes its incident edge, so the labels of these edges record the descent history. They are precisely the nonroot right-chain minima.

The grading argument of Theorem A(ii) applies: intermediate synchronised partitions can be realised by giving each block its minimum as image, which satisfies the enlarged bounds. The rank is the common number of blocks minus one. The history enumeration proves the asserted rank polynomial. ∎

6.3 Fixed plateaux, partial gamma-positivity, and PECKness

We now take m=2m=2 and ℓ=1\ell=1. For an ordinary Stirling permutation, let plat⁡(σ)\operatorname{plat}(\sigma) count the adjacent equal pairs. In its ternary tree this equals the number of empty middle slots. For 1≤p≤n1\leq p\leq n, let ℛn,p\mathcal{R}_{n,p} be the induced subposet of ℛn,1(2)\mathcal{R}^{(2)}_{n,1} whose corresponding words have pp plateaux. Equivalently, their trees have exactly q=n−pq=n-p middle edges.

The outer-slot involutions below realise the same orbit decomposition as the Gessel-tree Foata–Strehl action of Chen–Fu–Yan [7, Section 3 and Theorem 3.1]. Its partial gamma-positive enumerator is known; see also Ma–Ma–Yeh [18, Section 3]. Its compatibility with the kernel order yields Theorem G, which we now prove.

Proof of Theorem G.

A partition with ss blocks is the right-chain partition of a tree with qq middle edges if and only if s≥q+1s\geq q+1. Necessity holds because every middle child starts a nonroot right chain. Conversely, we choose qq nonroot block minima to be middle children and designate all the remaining nonroot block minima as left children. We attach the chain roots in increasing order. At a root vv, its designated slot is available at v−1v-1 earlier vertices, and at most v−2v-2 previously attached roots have used that slot type. An available parent therefore exists. This realizes the partition with exactly qq middle edges.

It follows that the possible block counts are q+1,…,nq+1,\ldots,n. Any intermediate partition between two comparable elements is realizable with qq middle edges. Hence covers are precisely comparable pairs whose block counts differ by one. A partition with more than q+1q+1 blocks can be coarsened by one merge and realised again; a partition with fewer than nn blocks can be refined by one split. Thus all minimal elements have q+1q+1 blocks, all maximal elements have nn blocks, and the stated grading follows.

We fix the parent relations of a ternary tree and every middle edge. We also fix the left–right order at vertices having both outer slots occupied. At a vertex with exactly one occupied outer slot, we forget whether its outer child is left or right; a middle child may still be present. The resulting object is called an outer-slot skeleton. If it has bb doubly occupied outer pairs and uu singly occupied outer pairs, then

n−1=q+2​b+u.n-1=q+2b+u.

Its orientations are indexed by S⊆[u]S\subseteq[u], recording the outer edges directed left. They have q+b+|S|q+b+|S| internal descents and hence rank b+|S|b+|S| in ℛn,p\mathcal{R}_{n,p}.

Moving a singly occupied outer edge from right to left deletes one right-chain edge and splits one kernel block. It is therefore an upper cover in the induced poset. Conversely, comparability between two orientations forces inclusion of their block-minimum sets, hence inclusion of the corresponding subsets SS. Each skeleton class is an induced Boolean subposet. Its endpoint ranks sum to 2​b+u=p−12b+u=p-1, so these classes form a symmetric Boolean decomposition. Applying the Boolean symmetric chain construction from Theorem E gives a symmetric chain decomposition of ℛn,p\mathcal{R}_{n,p}.

For the operator statement, we use the Boolean operators in (5.5) on each skeleton. Their diagonal operator satisfies

H​eS=(2​|S|−u)​eS=(2​ρp​(T)−(p−1))​eS.He_{S}=(2|S|-u)e_{S}=(2\rho_{p}(T)-(p-1))e_{S}.

The raising and lowering operators are supported on the covers just described. Their direct sums satisfy (5.3), so we can apply Lemma 5.2 to obtain PECKness. Finally, a skeleton contributes tb​(1+t)ut^{b}(1+t)^{u} to the shifted descent enumerator, giving (I.6). ∎

Example 6.2.

Take a ternary tree whose root 11 has middle child 22, and whose vertex 22 has right child 33. Its word is 122331122331. Moving the child 33 to the left produces 133221133221. The two words have two plateaux and respectively one and two internal descents, so they form a two-element chain in ℛ3,2\mathcal{R}_{3,2} with shifted ranks zero and one. The three plateau slices at n=3n=3 have descent enumerators

p321∑plat⁡(σ)=ptd⁡(σ)1+4​t+t2t⁡(4+4​t)t2.\begin{array}[]{c|ccc}p&3&2&1\\ \hline\cr\displaystyle\sum_{\operatorname{plat}(\sigma)=p}t^{d(\sigma)}&1+4t+t^{2}&t(4+4t)&t^{2}.\end{array}

Their sum is 1+8​t+6​t21+8t+6t^{2}. The separate symmetry centers explain why the full descent polynomial is not palindromic.

Remark 6.3.

The fixed-plateau theorem concerns one Stirling permutation. For synchronised tuples, a common descent history specifies whether each inserted label uses a left or middle slot, but does not specify which of the two. Thus simultaneous outer-slot flips need not preserve this family. For example, the pair (2211,1221)(2211,1221) has common history (1)(1); flipping its available outer edge gives (1122,1221)(1122,1221), with different histories. The stability theorem for arbitrary ℓ\ell therefore does not imply a corresponding fixed-plateau PECK or gamma theorem for synchronised tuples.
